title: User-published AI artifact pages get a separate serving domain by H1 2027
body: Huntress's FakeAgent write-up describes an attack that needed no vulnerability at all. Sponsored Bing ads running July 21-22 pointed at a genuine claude.ai URL — a public Artifact the attacker had published on Anthropic's own domain — which redirected to a fake ClaudeDesktop.exe that sideloaded SectopRAT with GPU-based payload decryption. Twenty-nine organizations were affected, the malicious page drew 7,100 views before takedown, and the registration email behind the redirect domain ties to at least ten others going back to December 2025, one of them previously seized in Operation Endgame. Nothing had to be breached: the ad network's destination review saw a legitimate first-party domain, and so did every reputation-scoring control downstream of it. The prediction is that at least one major vendor now serving user-published pages from its primary product domain — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or Microsoft — relocates that surface onto a separate registrable domain by H1 2027, a name browsers treat as a different site rather than as part of the product, and says publicly that abuse rather than performance drove the move. The structural force is that the rest of the web settled this question years ago. Content that arbitrary users can publish is served from its own registrable name — github.io for GitHub Pages, googleusercontent.com for Google's user files, dropboxusercontent.com for Dropbox — precisely so it cannot borrow the parent brand's reputation and cannot sit inside the parent's cookie and same-origin boundary. AI vendors skipped that step because sharing is a growth surface and hosting it on the main product domain made every published page look like the product itself; the security cost stayed theoretical until an operator monetized it. FakeAgent monetized it, and the bill falls on the one asset a publish feature cannot repair by itself — the domain reputation that ad networks, mail filters and endpoint tooling all read as a proxy for intent, and that an attacker can now rent for the price of a sponsored search slot. The same week's SharedRoot sandbox escape is the identical failure class one layer down: a trust boundary asserted by architecture rather than enforced by it. What falsifies the call is the cheap path holding. If through H1 2027 Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Microsoft all keep serving user-published pages from their primary product domains, and answer this class of abuse with faster takedowns, upload scanning, publish-rate limits and ad-network reporting alone, the prediction fails.

reasoning.because: Bing ads pointed at a real claude.ai Artifact that redirected to a fake installer; 29 orgs affected
reasoning.given: Untrusted pages on a vendor's own domain inherit the reputation ad networks and scanners trust
reasoning.so_that: A major vendor moves user-published pages to a separate registrable domain and names abuse as the reason
reasoning.landing: by H1 2027; Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or Microsoft ships the split
reasoning.plain_language: Crooks used a page published on an AI company's own website to spread malware, so those pages will move to a separate address.

summary: Bing ads pointed at a page an attacker had published on Anthropic's own domain, which redirected to a fake installer and affected 29 organizations. Untrusted user pages on a vendor's own domain inherit its reputation, so a major vendor should serve them from a separate domain by H1 2027.
